verses: For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm of David. Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have relieved my distress; show me grace and hear my prayer.
How long, O men, will my honor be maligned? How long will you love vanity and seek after lies? Selah
Know that the LORD has set apart the godly for Himself; the LORD hears when I call to Him.
Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still. Selah
Offer the sacrifices of the righteous and trust in the LORD.
Many ask, “Who can show us the good?” Shine the light of Your face upon us, O LORD.
You have filled my heart with more joy than when grain and new wine abound.
I will lie down and sleep in peace, for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.
title: Search Your Heart
season_line: Yesterday David woke up safe in the morning psalm; today he speaks the evening psalm, talking to people who have wronged him and then lying down in peace.
big_idea: Anger can be honest without turning sinful when you bring it to God and let His presence, not winning, be your good.
frame: Most of us don't carry dramatic enemies, but we do carry small grievances: a sharp word at breakfast, a coworker who took credit, a relative who always pokes the sore spot. Scripture never asks us to pretend we're not upset. It asks us to stop, get quiet before God, and let Him sort out what is just hurt and what is pride. Jesus Himself was angry without sinning, and Paul tells the church to settle anger before the sun goes down ({{Ephesians 4:26-27|Ephesians 4:26–27}}). Carry a slower posture today: feel it, name it to God, and refuse to let it pour out as spite.

glance.head: A cry to be heard
glance.line: David asks the God who has rescued him before to answer and show him grace again.

glance.head: Words to his accusers
glance.line: He confronts people who smear his name and reminds them the LORD has set apart His own and hears them.

glance.head: What to do with anger
glance.line: Be angry without sinning, get quiet on your bed, search your heart, and trust the LORD.

glance.head: Joy and peaceful sleep
glance.line: When others hunt for something good, David finds deeper joy in God's face and sleeps safe.

understand: Psalm 3 was a morning prayer; Psalm 4 is often read as its evening partner, and both end with David lying down to sleep. The setting may be the same hard season, when David's own people turned on him, but this psalm doesn't say. What it does show is a man whose reputation is being dragged through lies, speaking to his opponents and to God in the same breath.

Verse 4 is the heart of it. David tells angry people, likely including himself, to feel it without letting it become sin. Then comes the practical part: on your bed, search your heart and be still. Lie there and be honest before God instead of rehearsing the argument. Paul picks up this very line in {{Ephesians 4:26-27|Ephesians 4:26–27}}, warning that anger left to fester overnight gives the devil a foothold.

Thursday we saw Jesus look around in anger at hard hearts and then heal a man's hand ({{Mark 3:1-5|Mark 3:1–5}}). His anger served love; it didn't serve Himself. That's the kind of anger the psalm makes room for.

Verse 6 echoes the priestly blessing in {{Numbers 6:24-26|Numbers 6:24–26}}, where the LORD makes His face shine on His people. David's answer to the question of who can show us good is not a better harvest or a won argument. It's God's face turned toward us, and that brings a joy that lets him sleep.

word.gloss: This Hebrew word means to shake or be stirred up, whether with anger or fear. It names the inner trembling we feel when wronged, and the psalm says that feeling itself need not be sin.

god.short: Tonight in bed, name one frustration to God, then stay still a minute.
god.full: Before you fall asleep, tell God plainly what you're angry about today. Then ask Him to search your heart, and lie quiet for one full minute before you start explaining yourself.
god.why: David counsels this exact bedside practice in {{Psalm 4:4|Psalm 4:4}}.

together.short: Pray one line together: Lord, don't let us sleep angry with each other.
together.full: Before you leave the table, hold hands and one of you prays a single line: Lord, don't let us go to sleep angry with each other tonight.
together.why: Paul applies this psalm to everyday relationships in {{Ephesians 4:26|Ephesians 4:26}}.

others.short: Pray God's shining face over someone who's irritated you, then do one kindness.
others.full: Think of a coworker or relative, maybe someone you'll see at a gathering this week, who gets under your skin. Ask God to shine His face on them, then do one small kind thing for them.
others.why: Jesus tells us to pray for those who mistreat us in {{Luke 6:27-28|Luke 6:27–28}}.

tonight: When you're upset with me, what helps you get still and talk it out instead of stewing, and how can I make that easier?

more.line: Paul quotes Psalm 4:4 for daily life together.
